 Working from Home
1     As more and more professionals seek a better work-life balance and more companies adopt flexible policies to accommodate shifting workplace priorities, the working from home option is becoming increasingly viable. Employees see this as an ideal means to remain in the workforce and continue to be employed, thereby maintaining all the benefits of being part of an established company; while enjoying all the advantages of being based at home.                             5
2     By working from home, you save on many hidden costs associated with going to work such as costs of commuting car wear and tear; fuel, parking charges - and costs of maintaining and dry-cleaning an expensive professional wardrobe. Working from home offers the flexibility to determine your own work hours and work environment aspects such as lighting; temperature, and setting: It means you can basically work in the framework that suits you best and makes     10 
 you happiest and most productive. If you can choose your own work environment; you are able to determine a place with none of the unnecessary interruptions associated with the workplace; such as colleagues' teasing and unimportant meetings. Removed from the office stresses and distractions, professionals are often a lot happier and more productive.
3    The stress of commuting in bumper-to-bumper traffic at rush hour in many countries is   15 
 extremely counter-productive. It obviously leads to disgruntled workers who are already exhausted and worn out before they have even begun their day: This is especially true where the workplace is far from the office.
4    Often with long commutes, both physical and mental health are adversely affected: By working from home the commuting time saved enables you to resume physical exercise,  20 
 to go for a long walk for example before and after work or to join a local gym: Work and personal life balance, the aspiration of the modern professional, is often achieved and tuned to satisfaction through a working from home arrangement:
5    For many; the physical proximity to family and the convenience of being at home are tremendously comforting: For parents it can be especially comforting to know that they are      25 
 very near to their children and available should they be needed for any reason:
6    Working from home however; has its drawbacks. Often, professionals working from home complain of isolation and loneliness resulting from their removal from their bosses and co-workers: Since the workplace provides a location to meet people and make friends, professionals working from home have to be more creative and resourceful in getting to know   30 
 people and in staying in touch with their colleagues:
7    Although office distractions are avoided by working from home, different distractions may arise interruptions from children, neighbours, friends, family may be very disruptive and special efforts must be made to make it known that you are actually unavailable despite your physical presence at home. Added to these, is the difficulty in separating home from      35 
 professional work: The temptation to engage in household matters since you are at home is often very strong: Suddenly you may feel obliged to clean the home, do the shopping, the cooking; the home finances and the socializing all while meeting the full requirements of the job too. It is essential to draw the line between home and work so as to avoid both areas suffering:   40
8    Another disadvantage is that work does not really end: Since there is no-one looking over your shoulder enforcing strict hours, you may feel tempted to work endlessly.This pressure to
carry on working longer hours than you normally would may be compounded by the fact that you feel there are greater expectations made of you as a home-worker or by self-imposed pressures to prove yourself: Moreover; the lack of physical separation between home and     45 
 work may add to this pressure to work endlessly; not to mention the alienation from daily company developments: You may find yourself removed from important developments such as staff changes, new business, or changes in company direction. While working tirelessly in this self-imposed pressure, the danger of being overlooked for promotions and career development opportunities is quite real when you are away from the office. An open line of     50 
 communication with management and regular visits to the office are critical to prevent the out-of-sight-out-of-mind syndrome. SECTION 1 
 Passage 1 Raising sheep
1     Raising sheep can be a great option for farmers and others who do not have enough land
 to keep cattle but still want to raise some type of livestock. The general consensus amongst
 sheep farmers is that one can have four to six sheep per acre as opposed to one cow and
 her calf per acre. Sheep are social creatures and are happiest in a group setting, so it is
 recommended that one keeps a minimum of four to five together.      5 
2     Before starting any new pursuit; it is important to understand the costs involved.
 Fortunately, sheep can be relatively inexpensive to raise and the initial investment is loW.
 Start-up costs include the price of the sheep, fencing, and shelter. A farmer may even have the shelter and 
 fencing already set up. On-going costs include any sheep feed required and health costs,
 including vaccinations and visits. Sheep are lovable creatures and raising them does not       10 
 require a lot of expensive machinery. A mower may be needed to cut overgrown fields, but 
 proper pasture management should limit the need for this. Basic supplies will include a set of 
 clippers for shearing, and hoof trimmers.
3     Sheep do not require complex or expensive shelter. They can survive most of the time outside 
 provided there is some basic shelter from the wind and bad weather: Their housing can vary    15
 depending on your budget and your climate. The ideal accommodation is dry, open-sided, 
 and well ventilated. Hay, straw, or pine shavings used as bedding can provide extra warmth 
 and comfort for the sheep. 
4      Feeding sheep can be quite affordable: pasture grass is the main gource of food for the
 sheep herd, but sometimes you may have to supplement this with sheep feed and other        20 
 grains. Proper grazing management will not only reduce costs associated with supplement 
 feed, but it will also help manage overgrowth. It is important to keep a fresh supply of water 
 accessible at all times.  You should develop a timetable for rotating your sheep throughout 
 your pastures because, if left too long in one location, sheep can wreak havoc on your fields.
 Overgrazing of pastures can kill the grasses, lead to soil erosion and increase farm costs       25 
 associated with re-seeding. Sheep eat a variety of forages including weeds and brush.
 This is very beneficial to a producer because sheep do not require high-quality forages. Sheep 
 also eat grain that is lost in the field at harvest. They are versatile and can graze in various 
 environments such as rugged mountain areas and on land where crops cannot be produced.
 Wool breeds can also withstand the colder regions of the country: Sheep can frequently     30 
 have multiple births and can be raised on a limited number of acres. They also yield many 
 by-products that consumers use daily: Finally; sheep are produced for meat. 
5     As with the production of any product there are always drawbacks Consumers are not willing 
 to pay high prices for certain cuts of lamb, although less expensive cuts of lamb meat are 
 available. The public's meat preferences are heavily drawn to beef and chicken. Another     35 
 adverse factor is that the meat processing and marketing structure fluctuates. This means 
 that a sheep producer's enterprise may be profitable for one year but not the next, depending 
 on how many sheep are marketed at a given time relative to consumer demand. Currently, 
 there is not a high demand for wool clothing on the market. 
6     Unfortunately  sheep are easy prey for predators because they are unable to defend      40 
 themselves. They are also very susceptible to diseases, injury and various external 
 and internal parasites: Many of the parasites are deadly to sheep and can cost the producer a 
 lot of money. Because sheep are fragile animals, producers must carefully manage them 
 to prevent injuries. Another major issue is that labour costs for managing sheep are high 
 and much of the work involved with sheep production is seasonal, such as at shearing and      45 
 lambing times.

The writer describes a mysterious dream that a teenage boy; Alex; has while at a boarding school. The dream almost leads him into danger.
1     Alex was lying in bed, the moonlight spilling onto his covers. He took a look at his watch. It 
 was a quarter past two. He played again the dream he had just had. He thought about what 
 he had heard; the boarding Master laughing and a clicking sound. That was strange. What 
 had gone click? Had it actually been part of the dream? Suddenly, Alex was 
 completely awake. He got out of bed, went to the door; and turned the handle. He was right He had not    5 
 imagined the sound. While he was asleep, the door had been locked from the outside.
2     Something odd had happened, so Alex got dressed as quickly as possible and then knelt 
 down to examine the lock: He could make out bolts, one at the top and the other at the bottom. 
 They must have been activated automatically. One thing for sure, he was not going to get 
 out through the door: That left the window; but all the bedroom windows were fastened with a   10 
 steel rod that allowed them to open 20 centimetres but no more. Alex was so determined to 
 find out what was going on that he put his favourite Beethoven CD in the player and turned it 
 on. As it started spinning at a fantastic speed, he held his breath as he thrust the edge of his 
 CD against the steel rod. It took just a few seconds The CD cut through the steel rod like 
 a pair of scissors through a paper: The rod fell away, allowing the window to swing fully open.  15 
3     As it was snowing, Alex put on a sweater and a coat and then climbed out the window. 
 He was two floors up. Normally a fall from that height would have broken an ankle or a leg but it 
 had been snowing for the better part of ten hours and a white bank had built up against 
 the wall right beneath him: He lowered himself as far as he could, then let go. He fell through the 
 air and hit the snow, disappearing as far as the waist. Fortunately the bank had cushioned     20 
 him and muffled any sound that could have resulted from the fall. He was unhurt.
4     He climbed out of the snow and began to move around the side of the building, making for 
 the front; He would just have to hope that the main entrance wasn't locked too. He had just 
 made it to the side of the building when he heard the guards approaching, boots crunching. 
 There was nowhere to hide, so he threw himself face down onto the snow; hugging the     25 
 shadows. He could hear the guards talking softly but he didn't dare look up. He held his 
 breath, his heart pounding: They - walked past and rounded the corner: He was aware that he might not have much time, he had to move.
5     He lifted himself up and ran forward. His clothes were covered in snow and more flakes 
 were falling, drifting into his eyes. It was the coldest time of the night and, despite the short    30 
 stretch, Alex was already shivering uncontrollably as he stumbled towards the main door. 
 He suddenly felt apprehensive. What would he do if it was locked after all? 
6     Fortunately, the main door was unlocked. Alex pushed it open and slipped into the warmth 
 and darkness of the main hall: The fireplace was in front of him. There had been a fire earlier 
 in the evening and the burned-out logs were still smouldering in the hearth Alex held his      35 
 hands against the glow, trying to draw a little warmth into himself. Everything was silent. The 
 empty corridors extended into the distance, illuminated by a few bulbs that had been left on. 
 Only now did it occur to Alex that he could have been mistaken from the start. Perhaps he 
 had jumped too quickly to the wrong conclusion and there was nothing mysterious going on 
 at all.    40

Passage 1
 The origins of fashion
1    Fashion, in its broadest sense, is a particular style that is popular for a few months or 
 years. We speak of fashion in automobiles, furniture, design, music, literature and art. Most 
 commonly, however; fashion refers to a style of clothing that is worn at a given time but is 
 expected to change.
2   True fashions began to appear in Europe and Italy when a system of social classes developed   5 
 in the Middle Ages. At this time, Europeans began to classify one another into groups based 
 on such factors as wealth , ancestry and occupation. Clothing helped identify people as 
 members of a particular social class. Before then, only the wealthy and powerful concerned 
 themselves with the style of their clothes. But when the class system developed, the general 
 population began to compete for social status through fashion.     10 
3    One of the first true fashions appeared among young Italian men during the Renaissance (1300-1600). While their elders dressed in long traditional robes, young Italian males began 
 .wearing tights and short, close-fitting jackets  German soldiers set another early fashion 
 when they slashed their luxurious silk clothes with knives to reveal another colourful garment 
 underneath.   15
4     Before the 1800s, many countries controlled fashion with regulations called sumptuary laws, 
 which determined the amount of money people could spend on private luxuries. These laws were designed to preserve divisions among the classes and regulated fashion according 
 to a person's rank in society. In some countries, only the ruling class could legally wear silk, 
 fur and the colours red and purple. Other sumptuary laws forced people to buy products      20 
 manufactured in their own country to help the country's economy. An English law in the 1700s 
 prohibited people of all classes from wearing cotton cloth produced outside of England. But 
 the lure of fashion caused many people to break this law.
5      Often people imitate the style of a person or group with whom they identify: In the past, 
 many fashions originated in the upper classes and trickled down to the lower ones. Ordinary people     25 
 sometimes hoped to raise their social position by following the fashions of privileged people. 
 In a way, this still happens. But today celebrities such as singers and athletes, rather than 
 aristocrats, set fashions.
6    Fashion is also a form of non-verbal communication that provides a way for people to express 
 their identities and values. For example, in the 1960s, many young people rejected adult    30 
 values by rejecting mature styles of clothing. They adopted an international youth style that 
 included mini-skirts and mod jackets. These fashions appealed to young people because 
 many adults disapproved of them. However, eventually adults began copying them.
7    Fashions, however, do change for various reasons. When the standard of beauty changes, 
 fashion changes with it. For example, when physical fitness came to be recognised as a    35 
 requirement for good looks in the 1980s,people began to wear exercise and athletic clothing more often. 
8     Fashions considered  appropriate  for men and women have changed as standards of 
 masculinity and femininity have changed. Until the late 1700s, upper-class European men 
 dressed as elaborately as women: men looked ridiculous in brightly-coloured suits trimmed     40 
 with gold and lace. Their hats were decorated with feathers and they wore high-heeled shoes 
 and fancy jewellery. But, by the mid-1800s, men had abandoned colour and decoration in 
 favour of plain, dark, woollen suits. Until the early 1900s, European and American women 
 rarely wore trousers and their skirts almost always covered their ankles. However, 20 years 
 later, standards of feminine modesty had changed to a point that women began to wear both     45 
 trousers and shorter skirts:
9    A clothing style may become fashionable over time with many different groups. People began 
 wearing blue jeans in the 1850s when Levi Strauss & Company sold tough cotton workpants to 
 gold miners in California. Formerly, jeans functioned as ordinary work clothes. Approximately 
 a century later; American teenagers adopted blue jeans as a comfortable , casual youth    50 
 fashion. Young people during the 1960s wore blue jeans as a symbol of rebellious, 
 political and social beliefs. Some years, later when people no longer considered jeans rebellious, 
 expensive designer jeans became fashionable. Fashion obviously causes styles to change 
 for a variety of historical, psychological and sociological reasons.

Passage 2
 Scuba
1    My friends often describe me as a cynic. For the most part,they are right; as a rule, I reserve 
 expressing my feelings for the rare occasions when am particularly moved. Fortunately, 
 even the harshest cynics are surprised sometimes. 
2     Most people in my hometown know who Scuba is, but I would bet that ninety-nine percent 
 of those people do not know Scuba's real name. Scuba is a homeless man who lives at the    5 
 public library. He did not really attract my attention until several months ago; since then, 
 have found him impossible to ignore.
3     At about ten o'clock one Friday night; I left my house with the intention of buying a pizza at a 
 local restaurant. I grabbed my coat to shield myself from the chill air, the result of a cold front 
 and snow in the Drakensburg. The temperatures were close to zero and threatening to drop    10 
 even more. Before I reached the store, I  passed the library and noticed Scuba sitting on a 
 concrete bench. Stopping at a red light just beyond the library, attempted to force myself not to 
 look back at his cold, shivering form. With guilt welling up inside my chest for driving past 
 Scuba so many previous times and overlooking him, I could not make myself look away.
4    As the light turned green, sat for a moment and asked myself what I was going to do.    15 
 Then accelerated slowly, waiting for the car on my left to pass as I changed over to the 
 left lane. I made four left turns at four consecutive traffic lights until | approached the library 
 again and pulled into the library's parking lot. Even then I paused for a moment, before 
 eventually opening the car door; the cold air stung me like a quick slap to my face. Slowly 
 and uncertainly I walked towards Scuba      20 
5     The street was eerily quiet as | crossed. So was Scuba, staring at me unwaveringly, he said 
 nothing as approached. The crow's feet framing his eyes, the ridges in his forehead, and 
 the wrinkles in his cheeks still stand out in my mind. How many nights had he lain on that 
 bench , covering his face as the wind whipped against it? Now he hugged his body tightly. He 
 was wearing an old pair of blue jeans, a shirt that I couldn't see clearly, and a jacket that was    25 
 several sizes too small and clung to his body; its sleeves ending just above his pale wrists. 
 As I gave him the money in my wallet, he took it -slowly- and stared at it for a second in 
 disbelief. Although the street in front of the library is usually an amalgam of car hooters, 
 headlights, whining engines throughout the night, nothing disturbed the silence. Scuba's 
 head rose slowly, and he looked me in the eye with nothing but sincerity and kindness as he    30 
 uttered two simple words: Be blessed. 
6    In any situation, I always know what to say, but this time was I dumbfounded. It was 
 as though a thick cotton sock had been jammed into my throat to stop me from replying. 
 After several seconds, I muttered something unintelligible and shuffled across the street to drive 
 home    35
7     During that particularly snowy winter I 
 often thought of Scuba in his pitifully thin clothes. 
 I often drove by the library looking for Scuba. I was encouraged when I did not see him lying 
 on the concrete bench. I have not seen him outside at night for quite a while. After that first 
 encounter, I stopped and gave Scuba some money a tew more times. We exchanged names 
 and talked some more. These subsequent meetings made me question why I had been     40 
 stupefied when he had first thanked me. 
8    When I hear an evangelist in an expensive watch, a designer suit and a fancy haircut, talking 
 from his luxury home tell me that am blessed, I am never moved. Scuba's words are more 
 powerful because he has no home, often no shelter, yet he is neither bitter nor resentful. 
 It would be easy to succumb to anger and spite, but he does not. Because my offering is    45 
 so paltry, he could easily refuse it and ignore me, but he does not. For this reason, Scuba 
 deserves my sentiment.

 degenerative physical disorders because of its nerve-stimulating anti-oxidants and anti-      15 
 inflammatory properties.
3     Two other benefits result from drinking coffee, the first one wholly physical. There are a 
 number of diseases that can impact liver health including both liver cancer and cirrhosis.

 cancer. A number of studies have also demonstrated the strong role of acids present      20 
 in coffee in protecting the liver from damage at various levels: Less obvious perhaps

 important for our health because it reduces the stress we may otherwise feel. This stress 
 plays a major part in the development ot several conditions that can lead to serious illness or even death.     25 
4     Despite the outlined value of coftee, care must be taken t0 ensure that it is taken

5     Although coffee is safe in low to moderate amounts, caffeine itself stimulates bowel

6     Although coffee is known as a stimulant, it can have the opposite etfect and cause fatigue

 the ideal nourishment complete with vitamins and nutrients that are easy to digest.

 needs. Apart from providing basic nutrition, breast milk is hygienic and at the desirable 
 temperature. It is packed with the antibodies that offer protection against infections and 
 numerous common childhood illnesses. Whenever your baby nurses, he acquires a 
 healthy dose of the mother's   antibodies, which   boosts   immunity against

3     Breastfeeding is also emotionally healthy as it produces the naturally soothing

 embracing and stroking. On the whole all that sucking guarantees optimum oral 
 development.

 encourages the uterus to shrink back to its pre-pregnancy size. Since breastfeeding 
 burns between 300 and 500 extra calories every day, it may assist the mother to 
 naturally lose the baby weight faster. Exclusive breastfeeding can further delay

 challenges associated with it. A breastfeeding mother has less freedom as nobody gets

6     Breastfeeding necessitates healthy lifestyle choices; hence nursing mothers have to      40

Passage 2
 A Goose named Bat
 The goose came with our new house In Manare. That is what Grandpa told everyone 
 whenever he and my grandmother threw parties in our spaclous garden. Bat, a smooth, white 
 bird with a yellow beak that was often spotted with the remains of cabbage, was our family 
 pet for 27 years I never found her as captivating as other people did. When my classmates 
 came to visit, they would flock to the small mosey pond under our big mango tree. There,   5 
 they would peer over the steel gate and watch Bat, her wings tucked and her black, beady 
 eyes meditative as she peacefully paddled among the frogs ad fish.
2     My friends joked that we called her Bat because of the sound she made when she honked.
 She did it hundreds of times per day, telling us that she was hungry; that her pond needed 
 cleaning; or that the fairies were not too pleased with my naughty behaviour - or so my   10 
 mother's sister, Aunt Vicky, told me. 
3    Bat was not a friendly creature: Even to this day, I can still vividly recall how terrified I was of 
 her when I was younger. My nannies often told me stories of how the geese on the farms 
 could peck you black and blue. As much as I could, I stayed away from Bat, except when my 
 aunties handed me a dish of mashed pumpkin and told me to give her some dinner. I   15 
 remember hastily putting her meals by the gate ad running off as quickly as my little legs 
 could carry me.
4     Even as I grew older, did not dare lay a finger on her feathers. In fact, have very few 
 endearing memores of Bat. I do recall that she sometimes visited our swimming pool. After 
 collecting the dozens of feathers whenever Bat had been in the pool, I would tell my parents    20 
 that they were my quill pens.
5     In later years, Bat would walk through the old verandah, among the thick vines that had grown 
 on the marble pillars that held up the house. She lived through the grieving days when 
 Grandpa and Aunt Vicky breathed their last, and in the years when my nieces and nephews 
 were bom and we began planting flowers and picking mangoes from the trees once again.   25 
6     I would watch as she flapped her wings, in an attempt to fly during the stormy months, heavy 
 snows, and in the summer heat while she slept under cool, mossy trunks. My grandmother 
 used to tell me that Bat was a lucky bird and would live forever, just like the house. thought 
 that it was a silly idea, but some part of me believed, or at least hoped it was true. 
7     In the rush of my life , I was oblivious to the fact that the garden and pond had grown quieter, 30 /n and that Bat seldom came to the verandah. Someone occasionally mentioned that she was /n feeling ill, or that her age was taking its toll on her. did not think much of it, for I took it for granted that she would live forever.
8     One rainy afternoon, in June 2011, Bat finally let go. I was only 16 at the time. Overwhelmed 
 with emotion, I locked myself up in my room, full of grief  and completely confused. I realised   35 
 then that Bat did not only bring a sense of continuity to our family, but also slgnified that life.
 does go on in the midst of the beginning and the end, love and distress, happiness 
 and sorrow. No matter what, the house would stand and the family would too. It is silly to write 
 about a goose and even sillier to cry over one. But it is in stories like this that she, and we 
 too, will live forever.     40

1     As the frigid wind blew against my face, my nose and ears went numb. My legs and arms 
 were convulsing. Every step felt like thousands of needles were piercing into my legs. I 
 couldn t take it. In that moment I regretted not checking the weather reports. I " rationally" 
 assumed that the temperature would not drop below the twenties. Sure enough, the bone- 
 chilling breeze and white roads confirmed the weather dropped to five degrees Celsius. It felt    5 
 like I was in an Arctic plain.
2     It was a special weekend and my parents decided to take a trip to the National Park. On our 
 first night, we decided to visit the National Museum. As we were glancing around, my father 
 pointed to a massive poster for skiing beside a nearby fast-food cafe. I looked at my mother 
 and she responded, 'high five!'. We all could not believe how lucky we were      10 
3     The following morning, we got dressed and prepared to take on the freshly fallen powder.
 When we arrived at the snow-scooter company, we were informed that the cable car that 
 takes visitors to the top of the mountain, where they rent the snow-scooters, was under 
 maintenance and the only way to get up there was by hiking. Without giving it another moment 
 to register what we were about to get ourselves into, we paid the parking and gathered up a     15 
 few water bottles to stay hydrated as we hiked up.
4     The hike started from a parking lot next to a highly-travelled road. The trail was amidst the 
 woods that secluded one from the rest of the world where there were no roads, buildings, or 
 any infrastructure. I was in my own thoughts with just nature in sight, and only nature. At first , 
 nature had to adjust to my presence. The squirrels scattered away as I walked towards them,     20 
 and scurried up the trees. The birds silenced their chirping simultaneously ad tilted their 
 heads at a 180-degree angle to analyse what kind of aimal might be. Nature was hiding 
 from an outsider and watching. However, it was not long before nature continued what it was 
 doing. For the duration of the hike, I became one with nature. Following a snowy path, I could 
 vaguely distinguish the bright yellow marks that are meant to lead one through the wild, and     25 
 finally to the destination.
5     On my continuation of the hike, nature presented me with several pleasures and I devoured 
 it all as I made my way slowly up the mountain. I was taking it one step at a time, enjoying 
 the birds forming a band together, meshing their chirps with distinguishing pitches. As I 
 trekked, I allowed this new form of music to consume me. The vast number of trees provided     30 
 me with a variety of different scents . The scents mixed, giving a fresh air that made me 
 breathe easier; which was ironic as I suffer severely from respiratory infection - always feeling 
 like my lungs are getting squeezed, punctured, and punched. It was when got to the larger 
 boulders that knew I was getting closer to the top. To keep up with my father, I increased 
 my pace because I did not want to be the last one up. It did not last. Climbing up the slippery     35 
 rocks gave a bit of an exercise, but not an excruciating one. When I got to the end of the tree. 
 line , I knew that I was there. I did not rush though; because I wanted to experience every 
 bit of nature as much as possible. 
6     Once I reached the top of the mountain, my jaw clung to the ground. The world stretched for 
 miles and miles. It was almost as if I was everywhere at once. Thousands of frozen lakes and     40 
 rivers blended in with the white scenery of the snow. The sky was the colour of the sea on a 
 sunny yet cold day. Giant clouds rushed past me like ships on the ocean. What a splendour! 
 The tranquility allowed me to momentarily disconnect from the hustle and bustle of modern 
 life and gain a new perspective on what truly matters.
7     Yet, in the beautiful moment, my body was overwhelmed and sunk into a nearby rock. My     45 
lungs felt like they were about to explode. My lips were dry. My nose was running. My body 
 was frozen. But in that moment nothing mattered. The panoramic view made me feel 
 invincible. Forgetting all about the snow-scooter, I descended the mountain carrying with me 
 a feeling of satisfaction like no other.
